question: Who appoints notaries public in California?

options.why: Correct. Government Code §8200 gives the Secretary of State the power to appoint and commission notaries, and its Notary Public Section keeps the official records.
Wrong. The county clerk files the notary's oath and bond after appointment, but has no power to appoint anyone.
Wrong. The State Bar licenses and disciplines attorneys; it has no role in notary commissions.
Wrong. The Department of Justice processes the fingerprint background check, but the appointment itself comes from the Secretary of State.

explanation: The Secretary of State appoints and commissions California notaries.

question: How long is a California notary commission?

options.why: Correct. Government Code §8204 sets a four-year term, counted from the commission start date.
Wrong. Two years is half the actual term; California commissions run four years.
Wrong. Six years is longer than any California notary term; the statute sets four.
Wrong. Ten years is not a California notary term; the commission must be renewed every four years.

explanation: A California notary's commission runs four years.

question: How much education must a first-time California applicant complete?

options.text: A six-hour course approved by the Secretary of State
options.why: Correct. Government Code §8201 requires first-time applicants to complete a six-hour course approved by the Secretary of State before testing.
Wrong. Three hours is the refresher for timely renewals (and Florida's new-notary course), not the first-time California requirement.
Wrong. California makes education mandatory; no applicant may skip it.
Wrong. Forty hours is far beyond the six-hour requirement in §8201.

explanation: First-time applicants must complete a six-hour approved course.

question: A notary renewing before their current commission expires, who completed the six-hour course before, may take which course instead?

options.why: Correct. A notary renewing a current commission who has already taken the six-hour course may take the three-hour refresher instead.
Wrong. Even renewing notaries must complete approved education; only the length is reduced.
Wrong. A short video is not an approved course and doesn't satisfy §8201.

options.text: The six-hour course is always mandatory
options.why: Wrong. The six-hour course is required for first-time applicants; timely renewals have the three-hour option.

explanation: A notary renewing a current commission who previously completed the six-hour course may take a three-hour refresher.

question: What score is needed to pass the California notary exam?

options.why: Correct. The Secretary of State sets the passing score at 70% on the proctored exam.
Wrong. 60% falls short of the 70% passing score.
Wrong. 80% is more than required; 70% passes.
Wrong. 90% is far above the 70% passing score.

explanation: Applicants must score 70% or higher on the state exam.
source: Cal. Secretary of State exam guidance

question: What is the amount of the California notary bond?

options.why: Correct. Government Code §8212 requires a $15,000 surety bond, which protects the public up to that amount.
Wrong. $10,000 is the Texas bond amount, not California's.
Wrong. $7,500 is the Florida bond amount, not California's.
Wrong. New York requires no bond, but California does: $15,000 under §8212.

question: Within how many days of the start of the commission must the oath and bond be filed with the county clerk?

options.why: Correct. Government Code §8213 requires filing the oath and bond with the county clerk within 30 calendar days of the commission's start date.
Wrong. Ten days is shorter than the statute allows; the deadline is 30 calendar days.
Wrong. Sixty days is past the deadline; filing must happen within 30 calendar days.
Wrong. A year is far too long; missing the 30-day window means the notary can't act under that commission.

explanation: The oath and bond must be filed with the county clerk within 30 calendar days of the beginning of the commission term.

question: In which county are the oath and bond filed?

options.text: The county where the notary maintains their principal place of business, as shown on the application
options.why: Correct. §8213 ties the filing to the county of the principal place of business listed on the application.
Wrong. The notary can't simply pick a county; the principal place of business determines it.
Wrong. There is no single statewide filing county; each notary files where their principal place of business is.

options.text: The county where the notary was born
options.why: Wrong. Birthplace has nothing to do with where the oath and bond are filed.

explanation: The oath and bond are filed with the county clerk of the county of the notary's principal place of business.

question: May a California notary notarize before filing the oath and bond?

options.why: Correct. A notary isn't qualified to act until the oath and bond are filed; acts performed earlier are unauthorized.
Wrong. The 30-day window is the deadline for filing, not a period during which the notary may already notarize.
Wrong. There is no family exception; acting before qualifying is unauthorized for everyone.

options.text: Yes, if they have the seal
options.why: Wrong. Owning a seal doesn't confer authority; filing the oath and bond does.

explanation: A notary may not perform notarial acts until the oath and bond are filed.

question: Which applicants must undergo a background check with fingerprints?

options.why: Correct. §8201.1 requires every applicant, new or renewing, to submit fingerprints for a DOJ and FBI background check.
Wrong. Renewing notaries are fingerprinted too; there's no renewal exemption.
Wrong. Everyone is checked, not only people who disclose a record.
Wrong. Background checks are mandatory for all applicants.

explanation: All applicants are fingerprinted for a background check by the Department of Justice and FBI.

question: An applicant fails to disclose a past conviction on the application. What can result?

options.text: The Secretary of State may deny the application or revoke the commission for failing to disclose
options.why: Correct. Under §8214.1, failing to disclose an arrest or conviction is itself a ground to deny the application or revoke the commission.

options.text: Nothing, if the conviction was minor
options.why: Wrong. Even a minor conviction must be disclosed; hiding it is a separate violation.
Wrong. The consequence can be denial or revocation, not just a small fine.
Wrong. Exam scores are unaffected; the issue is honesty on the application.

explanation: Failing to disclose an arrest or conviction is grounds for denial or revocation.

question: A California notary moves their business address. How soon must they notify the Secretary of State?

options.why: Correct. Government Code §8213.5 requires notifying the Secretary of State within 30 days of an address change.
Wrong. A year is far too long; the deadline is 30 days.
Wrong. Waiting until renewal violates the 30-day notice rule.
Wrong. Five days is not the California deadline; §8213.5 allows 30 days.

explanation: Address changes must be reported to the Secretary of State within 30 days.

question: What is the civil penalty for willfully failing to notify the Secretary of State of an address change?

options.why: Correct. §8213.5 sets a civil penalty of up to $500 for willfully failing to report an address change.
Wrong. $10,000 is the cap for serious violations like false certificates, not address changes.
Wrong. $50 understates the statutory penalty of up to $500.
Wrong. The statute does impose a penalty, up to $500, for willful failure.

explanation: Willful failure to report an address change carries a civil penalty of up to $500.

question: A notary legally changes their name. What must they do?

options.text: File a name-change application with the Secretary of State within 30 days, then file a new oath and bond amendment and obtain a new seal
options.why: Correct. §8213.6 requires a name-change application to the Secretary of State within 30 days, then a new oath, a bond amendment and a new seal.

options.text: Keep using the old seal forever
options.why: Wrong. The old seal shows the old name and must be replaced once the amendment is processed.
Wrong. A name change is handled by amendment; the notary doesn't resign or retest.
Wrong. The county clerk can't amend a commission; the Secretary of State must be notified.

explanation: After a name change, the notary files an application with the Secretary of State within 30 days, then a new oath and bond amendment, and gets a new seal.

question: An employer paid for an employee's commission, seal and journal. Who owns the seal and journal?

options.text: The notary, even if the employer paid
options.why: Correct. Government Code §§8206–8207 make the seal and journal the notary's exclusive property, whoever paid for them.
Wrong. Paying for the tools doesn't give the employer ownership; they stay with the notary.
Wrong. The county clerk receives journals only when the commission ends without renewal, not as owner.
Wrong. The Secretary of State regulates notaries but doesn't own their seals or journals.

explanation: The seal and journal belong to the notary regardless of who paid for them.

question: Under Government Code §8202.8, what may an employer who paid for a notary's commission do?

options.text: Limit the notary, during business hours, to notarizations related to the employer's business
options.why: Correct. §8202.8 lets an employer who pays for the commission limit the notary, during business hours, to the employer's business transactions.

options.text: Use the notary's seal when the notary is away
options.why: Wrong. No one but the notary may use the seal, whoever paid for it.

options.text: Keep the notary's journal after the notary leaves
options.why: Wrong. The journal belongs to the notary and leaves with them.

options.text: Set fees above the statutory maximum
options.why: Wrong. Statutory fee limits bind the notary regardless of who employs them.

explanation: An employer who pays for the commission may limit the notary's services during business hours to transactions related to the employer's business.

question: Where may a California notary perform notarial acts?

options.why: Correct. A California commission is valid throughout the state, under §8200.

options.text: Only in the county of the principal place of business
options.why: Wrong. The county of the principal place of business is for filing; it doesn't limit where the notary can act.
Wrong. A California commission doesn't reach other states; acts must take place in California.
Wrong. Nothing ties the notary to the employer's office; they may act anywhere in California.

explanation: A California notary may act throughout the state.

question: What must a notary do with their journals when the commission expires without renewal?

options.text: Deliver them to the county clerk of the county where their oath is on file within 30 days
options.why: Correct. Government Code §8209 requires delivering all journals to the county clerk where the oath is on file within 30 days.
Wrong. Journals are evidence and must be preserved, never destroyed.
Wrong. Employers have no right to the journals; they go to the county clerk.
Wrong. The notary can't keep them; §8209 requires delivery to the clerk.

explanation: On resignation, revocation or expiration without renewal, journals go to the county clerk within 30 days.
